interview_metadata.name: Trisha Wheeler
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Hardin, Illinois, so my whole childhood was pretty small-town. Everybody knew whose truck was whose, and if you got in trouble at school, your mom heard about it before you got home. My family has always been tied to farm work and small businesses around Calhoun County, so I grew up around people who just did what needed doing. We went to a Methodist church, I did youth group, county fair stuff, and some 4-H things when I was younger. School was fine for me. I was more social and hands-on than bookish, but I did graduate high school, and I liked classes where I could actually do something practical. After high school I did not go straight into a four-year college. I worked, took some training, and ended up getting into dental assisting. That fit me better than I expected because it is people, organization, a little science, and a lot of moving around. I work as a dental assistant now, doing X-rays, sterilization, chairside help, patient notes in Dentrix, and calming people down when they are nervous. Family-wise, I am close with my parents and my younger brother, and I have a big friend circle here. I have never been married and I do not have kids. A lot of my life right now is work during the week and then softball, Zumba, karaoke, movie nights, church or family stuff, and random little road trips when I can afford it. The biggest thing in my life so far has probably been figuring out that I did not have to leave Hardin immediately to build something for myself, but I also do not have to stay exactly the same forever.

follow_ups.question: When you think about childhood in Hardin, what memories come up first?
follow_ups.response: Summer evenings mostly. Riding around with cousins, going to the county fair, helping set up tables at church dinners, and being outside until it got dark. It was not fancy, but it felt like people were always around.

follow_ups.question: Who was most influential for you growing up?
follow_ups.response: My mom, probably, because she kept everybody on track and taught me to talk to people kindly. My dad taught me the practical side, like show up, work hard, and do not act helpless.

follow_ups.question: What made dental assisting feel like a fit?
follow_ups.response: I like that it is busy and personal. I can take an X-ray, turn a room over, joke with a patient, and help the dentist all in one hour. I do better when I am not sitting still all day.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes. After high school I really did not know what I was doing. Some of my friends were leaving for college, some were already working full time, and I felt kind of behind even though I was only eighteen. I could have just bounced between jobs, or I could have tried school without a plan, which scared me because of money. A woman from our church worked at a dental office and told me they needed someone who was good with people and willing to learn. I started shadowing, then helping with front desk and sterilization, and I liked the rhythm of it. The crossroads was deciding to take it seriously instead of treating it like a temporary job. Once I did that, I started learning radiographs, chairside procedures, infection control, and office software. It gave me confidence because I had a skill people actually needed.

follow_ups.question: What was the first sign that this was more than just a temporary job?
follow_ups.response: I remember helping a really anxious older patient through an appointment, and afterward she squeezed my hand and said I made it easier. That stuck with me.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone push you toward that choice?
follow_ups.response: My parents encouraged it, but they did not force me. The biggest push was honestly seeing that I could learn it and not feel lost.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: At first it just happened. I needed work and the dental office needed help. But after a few months I made a conscious choice to stay with it, get better, and think of it as a career path instead of just a paycheck.

follow_ups.question: What did that conscious choice look like day to day?
follow_ups.response: I started asking more questions, writing little notes after procedures, and volunteering to learn X-rays instead of waiting to be told.

follow_ups.question: Did you give up anything by choosing that path?
follow_ups.response: A little bit of the freedom my friends had. I had to be up early and be dependable, even after late karaoke nights.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. I think more clear career guidance after high school would have helped. Not everybody needs a four-year degree, but I wish someone had laid out dental assisting, hygiene programs, certificates, costs, and what jobs actually pay around here.

follow_ups.question: Who did help the most?
follow_ups.response: The church friend who connected me to the office, and then the lead assistant who trained me without making me feel dumb.

follow_ups.question: What support would help you now?
follow_ups.response: Help figuring out radiography certification and maybe community college requirements for dental hygiene.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner right now, and I do not have children. I have dated, but nothing that turned into living together or marriage. My parents are very important to me. My mom is the person I call when I am stressed or when I need someone to tell me if I am being dramatic. My dad is quieter, but if my car makes a weird sound or I need help moving furniture, he is there. I also have a younger brother, Cody, who is twenty. He works locally and is still figuring out his direction, and we are close in that sibling way where we tease each other constantly but would show up fast if one of us needed something. I have grandparents and aunts and uncles around the county too, so family is not just people I see on holidays. It is more like people I run into at the grocery store, at church, at the fair, and sometimes at my softball games.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your parents?
follow_ups.response: Usually at least once a week, sometimes more. Sunday lunch happens pretty often if everyone is around.

follow_ups.question: What role do you play in the family?
follow_ups.response: I am the social one and the one who will organize a birthday dinner, though I might forget the napkins or be five minutes late.

follow_ups.question: Are you hoping to have a partner or children later?
follow_ups.response: Eventually, yes, if it is the right person. I am not rushing kids right now because I want to get steadier in my career first.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My immediate family is mainly my mom, dad, and my brother Cody. I am close with all of them, though Cody and I bicker over silly stuff.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk to Cody every day?
follow_ups.response: Not every day, but several times a week, usually texting memes or asking each other favors.

follow_ups.question: Do you have stepfamily or half siblings?
follow_ups.response: No, not in my immediate family.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My friends are a huge part of my life. My closest friend is Kayla; we do Zumba together and she is usually my passenger for weekend drives. My softball team is another circle, especially Jenna and Marcus, because we practice together and end up at the sports bar watching Cubs games. I also have a karaoke group that overlaps with work friends sometimes. We meet at bars or community events, and I have made extra money helping host karaoke nights. Those friends keep me from getting too stuck in my own head.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your closest friends?
follow_ups.response: Kayla I see at least once or twice a week. Softball people are weekly in season, and karaoke friends are usually Friday or Saturday nights.

follow_ups.question: What do your friends count on you for?
follow_ups.response: I am usually the one who gets people laughing and says yes to plans. They also ask me dental questions, which is funny.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Hardin, zip code 62047, and it is very much a small river town. You have the Illinois River close by, farm fields, older houses, churches, local shops, and people who wave even if they only sort of know you. There is not a big-city nightlife or tons of restaurants, so you make your own fun. A normal errand can turn into three conversations because you run into somebody's aunt or your old teacher. I like that part, though sometimes it means privacy is limited. It is quiet most nights, and the pace is slower than places like St. Louis or even some bigger towns nearby.

follow_ups.question: What places do you go most in town?
follow_ups.response: The grocery store, church, the community center, the river area, and wherever softball or karaoke is happening.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: Yes, at least casually. People notice if your car has not moved or if you have a package sitting out too long.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe. I lock my doors and use common sense, but I do not usually feel scared walking to my car or coming home late.

follow_ups.question: Are there times you feel less safe?
follow_ups.response: Mostly late at night after being out, especially if I am by myself in a parking lot.

follow_ups.question: What makes it feel safe?
follow_ups.response: Knowing people nearby and knowing someone would notice if something seemed off.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is community, family, and quiet. The downside is fewer job options, everybody knowing your business, and having to drive for certain stores, doctors, or entertainment.

follow_ups.question: Do you see yourself staying there?
follow_ups.response: I see myself keeping ties here, but I might move to a bigger nearby town if school or work makes sense.

follow_ups.question: What would you miss if you left?
follow_ups.response: The familiar faces and being close to the river and my family.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now I rent a small two-bedroom place with my friend Kayla. She works at a bank branch in a nearby town, and we split rent and utilities. It is not perfectly tidy because both of us are busy, but we keep the kitchen decent and try not to let laundry take over. We each have our own room, and the living room is where friends sometimes come for movie nights.

follow_ups.question: How did you and Kayla decide to live together?
follow_ups.response: We were both tired of living with family but did not want to afford rent alone, so it was practical and easy.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide chores?
follow_ups.response: Not in a strict chart. She is better with bills and I cook more, and then we both do panic cleaning if people are coming over.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just me and Kayla on the lease.

follow_ups.question: How long is the lease?
follow_ups.response: It is a one-year lease.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect that arrangement to continue?
follow_ups.response: Probably for now, unless one of us gets a big job change.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Friends might crash on the couch after karaoke or a movie night, but nobody regularly stays here.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month.

follow_ups.question: Is it usually planned?
follow_ups.response: Usually not. It is more like someone is tired and it is easier than driving.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody like that.

follow_ups.question: No college student away from home tied to the household?
follow_ups.response: No, just us two.

follow_ups.question: No one hospitalized or away for work?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Thursday are mostly work days. I am usually up around 6:30, at the dental office by 7:45 or 8, and done around 5 depending on patients. Fridays are a little lighter or sometimes half days, unless we are catching up. Tuesday night is usually Zumba at FitFusion Studio. During softball season I have practice or games one evening a week with the Shawnee Valley Co-ed Softball Club. Some nights I cook, some nights I eat leftovers, and some nights it is pizza because I did not plan. Weekends are more social: karaoke, movie nights, church sometimes, family lunch, hiking, fishing, or a quick road trip if money and weather line up.

follow_ups.question: What is your most predictable day?
follow_ups.response: Tuesday, because work then Zumba is pretty set.

follow_ups.question: What is your least predictable day?
follow_ups.response: Saturday. It can be laundry and groceries, or it can turn into Nashville plans if somebody gets an idea.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a dental assistant at a general dental office. Most weeks I work about 38 to 40 hours, Monday through Friday, with some early mornings. I help set up rooms, sterilize instruments, take intra-oral radiographs, assist during fillings, crowns, extractions, and orthodontic checks, and update patient records in Dentrix. I also sometimes help with scheduling or calling patients when the front desk is slammed. On the side, not every week, I sometimes help host karaoke events for a little gig money.

follow_ups.question: What part of the dental job takes the most energy?
follow_ups.response: Keeping up when we are behind schedule and still being calm with patients.

follow_ups.question: How often do you do karaoke gigs?
follow_ups.response: Maybe one or two times a month, depending on who needs help and whether I am free.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help my parents sometimes, mostly errands, lifting things, or helping my mom with events at church. I volunteer at the county health fair in the summer doing oral hygiene education, usually showing kids brushing and flossing basics. At home I cook a few nights a week and try to meal prep, though I am not perfect at it. I also keep track of my own certification planning because I want to get my dental radiographer certification within the next year.

follow_ups.question: What does volunteering at the health fair look like?
follow_ups.response: We set up a table with toothbrushes, floss, pamphlets, and little demonstrations for kids and parents.

follow_ups.question: When do you work on certification planning?
follow_ups.response: Usually Sunday evenings when I am trying to get my week together.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is I have been trying to be more structured. I started putting workouts and meals in my phone calendar because I kept overbooking myself. At work, we also changed some sterilization flow and scheduling, so I have been learning a tighter routine for room turnover. I am still a little scattered at home, but I am getting better about packing lunch instead of buying food.

follow_ups.question: What made you start using your phone calendar more?
follow_ups.response: I double-booked a softball practice and a family dinner, and everybody made fun of me, so I finally admitted I needed help.

follow_ups.question: Has packing lunch saved money?
follow_ups.response: Yes, not huge amounts, but enough that I notice.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so that does not apply to me. I hear about school routines from friends with kids, but I am not managing that myself.

follow_ups.question: Do children ever factor into your schedule through family or friends?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I help babysit a cousin's kid for a couple hours, but it is not a regular responsibility.

follow_ups.question: Does not having children affect your flexibility?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I can say yes to evening plans or extra work more easily than my friends who are parents.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have been pretty limited. I have been pulled over once for rolling through a stop sign and got a warning. In Hardin, you tend to know officers or know someone's family member who is an officer, so it feels personal in a small-town way. I have not had a scary encounter myself.

follow_ups.question: How did that traffic stop feel?
follow_ups.response: Embarrassing more than scary. I was nervous, but it was quick.

follow_ups.question: Do you generally trust local law enforcement?
follow_ups.response: Locally, mostly yes, though I know that is not everybody's experience.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly seeing them at community events, traffic after the fair, or coming into the clinic as patients. One officer came to a school safety thing when I was younger, but nothing dramatic.

follow_ups.question: Do police feel visible in your town?
follow_ups.response: Visible, yes, but not in a big-city way. More like at events or driving through town.

follow_ups.question: Have friends had different experiences?
follow_ups.response: A couple friends have had speeding tickets or party noise warnings, but nothing major that I know of.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I do not have immediate family who have been arrested. I know acquaintances who got DUIs, but not people I am extremely close to.

follow_ups.question: Did those DUI situations affect your social circle?
follow_ups.response: Mostly it made us more careful about rides after going out.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about that openly?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially after karaoke nights. We try to make sure nobody drives if they should not.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections, and I am trying to be better about local elections. When I was first old enough, I skipped one local election because I did not feel informed, but now I think local stuff actually affects daily life a lot. I do not follow politics every day, but I usually ask my parents, read a little online, and look at candidates before voting.

follow_ups.question: What motivates you to vote?
follow_ups.response: Feeling like I should have some say, especially on health care, jobs, schools, and local services.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you from voting sometimes?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, feeling like I do not know enough or that the choices are frustrating.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as moderate, maybe a little independent. I grew up around more conservative people, and I still value personal responsibility, work, family, and not wasting money. But working in health care has made me more aware that people can work hard and still struggle to pay for care. I care about dental care being affordable, rural clinics staying open, and people getting practical help without a bunch of shame attached to it. On social issues, I am probably more live-and-let-live than some older relatives. I do not like when politics becomes people just yelling online. I am not deeply attached to either party. I look at the person and the issue, though I know that sounds like what everybody says.

follow_ups.question: What issues matter most to you personally?
follow_ups.response: Health care access, jobs in rural areas, education or training after high school, and keeping communities like ours from drying up.

follow_ups.question: Do your views match your family?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat, but not completely. My parents lean more Republican than I do.

follow_ups.question: Where do you get political information?
follow_ups.response: Local news, Facebook links I double-check, conversations with family, and sometimes candidate websites.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have gotten less automatic about agreeing with whatever people around me say. Working with patients changed that because I see all kinds of people: older folks on fixed incomes, parents without dental insurance, people embarrassed about not being able to pay. I used to think assistance programs were mostly about people not trying hard enough, but now I think it is more complicated. I still believe people should do what they can for themselves, but I am more open to practical support systems.

follow_ups.question: Was there a patient story that changed your mind?
follow_ups.response: A woman delayed treatment for months because she could not afford it, and by the time she came in she was in real pain. She worked two jobs.

follow_ups.question: Did the pandemic period affect your views?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it made me think more about health workers, public health, and how fast people's finances can change.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say it affected me somewhat. I live in a mostly white rural area, so it is not something I grew up talking about in a deep way. But seeing videos and hearing people talk about policing made me realize I had assumed my experience was normal for everyone, and it is not. I did not become an activist, but I did start listening more and trying not to dismiss things just because they are not my day-to-day life.

follow_ups.question: What did you find hardest to understand at first?
follow_ups.response: How different people's experiences with police can be depending on race and place.

follow_ups.question: Did conversations in your town feel open or tense?
follow_ups.response: Mostly tense or quiet. People had opinions, but a lot of them did not want to argue.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the issues are real, even if people disagree about the movement or slogans. I think police have hard jobs, and I also think accountability matters. Those two things can both be true. I have been thinking more about how systems work differently for people, including in health care. Even in dental care, people with less money or fewer resources get treated later and suffer more.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about it through a health care lens often?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because that is where I actually see inequality up close.

follow_ups.question: Has it changed how you treat patients?
follow_ups.response: I try to be careful not to assume why someone missed appointments or delayed care.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think I am still learning. Growing up where I did, race was talked about like it was mostly a city issue or a history issue, and I do not think that is right anymore. I think the U.S. has made progress, but there are still big differences in opportunity, treatment, and trust. I try to listen more than talk because I know I have blind spots.

follow_ups.question: Where do you feel you have learned the most?
follow_ups.response: From reading personal stories and talking with coworkers or patients who have different backgrounds.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable discussing race?
follow_ups.response: Not always. I worry about saying something wrong, but I think avoiding it completely is worse.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked with friends and family. I have not joined protests. I have shared a couple articles or posts, but I am careful because social media arguments get ugly fast.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk with most about it?
follow_ups.response: Kayla and a couple coworkers, because they are willing to have a real conversation.

follow_ups.question: Have family talks changed anyone's mind?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a little, but usually it is more about understanding where each other is coming from.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friend group is mixed in opinions. Some are pretty supportive of reform, some think the movement went too far, and some just avoid the topic. My parents are respectful but more skeptical of national movements. At work, people mostly keep it professional, but you can tell folks have opinions. I think most people close to me care about fairness, but they disagree on what the problem is and what would fix it.

follow_ups.question: Does it cause conflict in your friendships?
follow_ups.response: A little, but we usually know when to stop before it ruins the night.

follow_ups.question: Do younger people around you discuss it differently than older people?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Younger people are usually more open to talking about systemic racism, while older relatives focus more on individual behavior.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am healthy. I am active with softball, Zumba, and line dancing, and I try to eat pretty well during the week. I do not have any major chronic condition. My weaknesses are sleep, stress eating, and sometimes overdoing it with late nights. Working in dental care also makes me pretty serious about brushing, flossing, and getting cleanings.

follow_ups.question: What does a healthy week look like for you?
follow_ups.response: Three workouts or active things, packed lunches, enough water, and getting to bed before 11 most nights.

follow_ups.question: What usually throws that off?
follow_ups.response: Karaoke nights, busy work days, or saying yes to too many plans.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy because my friends like active stuff and I enjoy cooking. It is hard because my schedule gets packed and cheap convenience food is tempting. If I am tired after work, pizza sounds way better than chopping vegetables.

follow_ups.question: What healthy meals do you actually make?
follow_ups.response: Quinoa bowls with grilled chicken, black-bean tacos with cilantro and lime, and sometimes salmon with miso glaze.

follow_ups.question: What helps you stick with exercise?
follow_ups.response: Classes and teams. If someone expects me there, I show up.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge. I sprained my ankle sliding into base during softball last summer, and I had to stay off it for a little while. I also had some back and shoulder soreness from standing and leaning at work, so I started paying more attention to stretching and posture. No major diagnosis or broken bones.

follow_ups.question: Did the ankle sprain affect work?
follow_ups.response: A little. I wore a brace and tried not to run around the office too fast.

follow_ups.question: Did you see a doctor for it?
follow_ups.response: I went to urgent care to make sure it was not broken.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: For me, health problems have not seriously gotten in the way. The ankle slowed me down, and occasional soreness makes me tired, but I can work and do my normal responsibilities.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever missed work for health reasons?
follow_ups.response: Just a sick day here and there, nothing long.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about injury because of work or sports?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly because I need to be on my feet at work.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: A little. My grandma has had some blood pressure and mobility issues, and my mom helps her a lot. I help with rides or errands sometimes. It has not taken over my life, but it reminds me that health can change fast. It also makes me think about how hard it is for older people in rural areas to get to appointments.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help your grandma?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a month, more if my mom is busy.

follow_ups.question: Does your dental background make family ask health questions?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly tooth and gum questions, or whether something looks like it needs a dentist.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have insurance through work, but it is not amazing. I can get basic care, but I still think about cost before making appointments. I have delayed things like physical therapy for soreness because I did not want the bill. Dental care is easier for me because I work in the field and know where to go, but medical care can mean driving and waiting.

follow_ups.question: What care have you delayed?
follow_ups.response: Mostly physical therapy or extra visits for muscle soreness.

follow_ups.question: What makes rural health care difficult?
follow_ups.response: Distance, fewer specialists, and appointments filling up fast.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing formal like indigenous medicine. My family does normal home remedies, like honey tea for a sore throat, heating pads, Epsom salt baths, and my grandma swears by certain rubs for sore joints. I have gone to a chiropractor once for back tightness, but I still trust regular medical care for serious things.

follow_ups.question: Do you use supplements?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes vitamin D or protein powder, but I am not strict about it.

follow_ups.question: Who recommends home remedies in your family?
follow_ups.response: Usually my grandma or my mom.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially, mostly on weekends at karaoke or watching games, but not every day.
